Material is safer than synthetic:

"Those using material cutting boards in their home kitchens were less than half as likely as average to contract salmonellosis (odds ratio 0.42, 95% confidence interval 0.22-0.81), those using synthetic (plastic or glass) cutting boards were about twice as likely as average to contract salmonellosis (O.R. 1.99, C.I. 1.03-3.85); and the effect of cleaning the board regularly after preparing meat on it was not statistically significant (O.R. 1.20, C.I. 0.54-2.68)."

The main point is that plastic chopping boards get all hacked up and bacteria find grooves and nooks to hide. 

Wood absorbs the bacteria, but then when the board dries, this kills the bacteria. And wood boards don't get hacked up as easily. 

In the end, it seems wood is better for home for this reason. Just wash and rinse, and I like to clean with a bit of salt and vinegar, then leave to dry.

It avoids tax and artificially inflates earnings per share etc.

EDIT:  Because a lot of people have asked how it avoids tax. 

Let's say I'm going to return $1bn to shareholders.   

The company could either do this as a dividend, which would then be taxed at 15%.  So (let's assume it works out to $100 per share) each shareholder receives $85 net and the taxman gets a total of $150m.

Alternatively, the company issues a buyback for $1bn worth of its stock.  This reduces the companies overall issued stock by (let's say) 10%.  Each person that sold shares receives the full face value of each of their shares sold without dividend tax, and the overall value of the shares they continue to hold is artificially increased (because they now hold the same percentage of the company, but each individual share is worth a slightly bigger percentage of the company).  

You've just avoided $150m in tax.  Yes on subsequent share sales, you could then be charged tax on the incremental increase in the value of each individual share (in which case, in a perfect world, the tax is just deferred).  But maybe you don't sell; maybe performance next year isn't as good and you sell at the original stock price.  Maybe there are all sorts of other things that mean that the incremental value of the share buyback on the value of each share isn't fully realised and therefore the tax on what is a dividend isn't paid.

I'm being slightly silly above, because yes it is down to our playing style.

People remember Hawthorn for the style we played when we won our flags - elite footskills, control the ball, control possession, precision going down the ground to slice people open.  Hell, even Gary Lyon during the North game was talking about us as if that's the way we play (moron).

Actually for a couple of years, we've played more of a territory game.  The idea is to get it inside 50 and try and lock it in.  You can see we have a lot of i50 entries, but a lot of them are garbage (much to my chagrin), because the tactic seems to be to play for territory rugby style, and then rely on our defensive structures to make it hard for teams to rebound.

This was very effective against Richmond, where they really struggled to get their rebound and run game going against our defensive structures.  It was also effective against North for 3 1/2 quarters.

It does mean fewer marks though, as the idea isn't to chip it around and find a precision entry, but rather get it in as quick as possible before their defense can set up properly and then lock it in.

It also must be very tiring, as we are regularly running out of legs at the end of games, as can be seen against the Tigers and North in particular.

Factor in the bulk of our contested marking opportunities were directed at Tim "always gets two hands to the ball; always drops it" O'Brien, Mitch Lewis not yet adjusting to the pace of AFL football, a very short midfield that don't provide much in the way of marking power, and you get low marking numbers.  All of our best marks are in defence, actually (particularly Sicily and Big Boy).
